what: The new dependencies T1209 introduced, recorded because docs/40_OPEN_SOURCE_LICENSES.md:7 asks for it:
"任何新增依赖必须记录 license、版本、用途、替代方案；高 copyleft/商业限制依赖需显式 ADR/法务确认".
What counts as "new" here: a package or scanner that this task added to the repository. Reused pins
(eslint 9.39.5, which apps/web already declares) are listed too, marked as such, so a reader cannot
mistake the row's toolchain for something the tree already had.
None of these is a runtime dependency of the product. They are scanners and their support packages;
nothing here is compiled into or shipped with the API, the web app or the adapter. The licences are
recorded for the same reason the SBOM records them — an inventory a reader can check — and every
entry below was read from the installed package's own licence file, not inferred from a registry page.
The versions are the pins in ops/security/tool-versions.sh; `make security-tools` installs exactly
them, and each gate row asserts the version it actually ran.

dependencies.name: gosec
dependencies.purpose: docs/23 §11 asks for SAST at every Release. gosec is the Go static analyser: it builds the package set and reports G-rules (hardcoded credentials, weak crypto, unsafe pointer/reflect use, unhandled errors on security-relevant calls, file permissions) as a JSON report this repository parses into a per-finding baseline.
dependencies.why_this_one: It is the Go ecosystem's standard SAST tool and the only one that both understands a multi-module Go repository and emits machine-readable output with a stable rule id per finding — the property the per-finding baseline depends on. v2.29.0 specifically: earlier 2.x releases fail to build against Go 1.27 (the toolchain CLAUDE.md §7 pins).
dependencies.alternatives: semgrep (single tool for three languages, larger rule set, a Python/OCaml toolchain to install, and its ruleset is a moving target unless pinned by commit); CodeQL (strongest analysis, but it needs a database build in a GitHub runner whose licensing differs for private repositories); staticcheck (already in this tree — correctness, not security rules, so it is not a substitute).
dependencies.license_check: Apache-2.0 is on the allowlist in ops/security/license-allowlist.json. No copyleft, no use restriction, no ADR required; it is not a distributed dependency of the product at all.

dependencies.name: bandit
dependencies.license_witness: the installed distribution's METADATA (uv tool install bandit==1.8.6): Name: bandit / Version: 1.8.6 / License: Apache-2.0
dependencies.purpose: The Python face of docs/23 §11's SAST: a scan of services/scientific-adapter/src for the classic Python security rules (subprocess with shell=True, unsafe deserialization, hardcoded passwords, weak hashing, assert used for control flow).
dependencies.why_this_one: PyCQA's bandit is the de-facto Python SAST tool, it is packaged as a single CLI, and it emits the same JSON shape this repository's report parser needs (file, line, rule id, severity, confidence).
dependencies.alternatives: semgrep (as above); pylint's security plugin (a linter's subset, weaker rules); ruff's `S` rules (already available in this tree via ops/ci/ruff.toml — the closest substitute, and the reason the adapter's ruff config is worth keeping in view: it covers a small overlapping subset with no per-finding baseline).
dependencies.license_check: Apache-2.0, on the allowlist. No ADR required.

dependencies.name: eslint-plugin-security
dependencies.purpose: The rule set behind the TypeScript/JavaScript face of SAST: detect-eval-with-expression, detect-non-literal-regexp, detect-object-injection, detect-child-process, detect-unsafe-regex and the rest of the plugin's recommended set — each forced to "error" in the SAST config, with a floor on the number of rules so a plugin upgrade that silently dropped rules would fail the config load rather than narrow the scan.
dependencies.why_this_one: It is the maintained eslint-community security rule set; eslint is already this repository's linter, so the Node face adds rules to a tool the tree runs rather than a second lint engine.
dependencies.alternatives: eslint-plugin-no-unsanitized (DOM sinks specifically; complementary, smaller); semgrep's TypeScript rules (a second engine); adding the plugin to apps/web's own eslint config (rejected: it would put a security rule set into the app's config, where `next lint` and any per-file disable comment could weaken it — so it lives in tests/security/node-tools with its own config and its own lockfile).
dependencies.license_check: Apache-2.0, on the allowlist. No ADR required.

dependencies.name: typescript-eslint
dependencies.purpose: Supplies the TypeScript parser and the typed lint configuration the SAST config runs under. Without it, eslint's default parser rejects every .ts/.tsx file as a parse error — the first version of this row reported 103 fatal parse errors and no findings, which is exactly the shape of a green-looking scan that measured nothing.
dependencies.why_this_one: It is the parser eslint itself documents for TypeScript, maintained by the typescript-eslint project, and it is the only parser that produces the AST the security rules need.
dependencies.alternatives: @typescript-eslint/parser directly (the same packages, without the aggregate entry point this config imports); oxlint (fast, but no eslint-plugin-security rule compatibility).
dependencies.license_check: MIT, on the allowlist. No ADR required.

dependencies.name: typescript
dependencies.kind: compiler (support package, peer of the parser)
dependencies.purpose: The compiler API the TypeScript parser loads. Pinned to the same 5.9.3 the web workspace builds with, so the SAST scan parses the sources the build compiles.
dependencies.why_this_one: It is the workspace's own compiler version; a different one here would mean the security scan reads a different language version than the build.
dependencies.alternatives: None — it is a hard requirement of the parser. Note it is a dependency of the isolated tests/security/node-tools project, not of apps/web, which keeps pnpm-lock.yaml untouched.
dependencies.license_check: Apache-2.0, on the allowlist. No ADR required.

dependencies.name: eslint
dependencies.kind: lint engine (REUSED — already declared by apps/web)
dependencies.purpose: The engine the security rules run on. Already a devDependency of apps/web at this exact version; the SAST toolchain installs its own copy inside tests/security/node-tools so the security rule set cannot be weakened from the application's config.
dependencies.why_this_one: Reusing the version the tree already runs avoids a second eslint in the workspace.
dependencies.alternatives: Adding the security plugin to the web workspace's eslint config — rejected, see eslint-plugin-security above.
dependencies.license_check: MIT, on the allowlist, and not a new dependency.

dependencies.name: cyclonedx-gomod
dependencies.purpose: docs/25 §1 item 10 asks for an SBOM per Release and docs/40:3 asks for the real versions and licences to be generated and checked in CI. This is the Go face: it reads go.mod, resolves the module graph and emits a CycloneDX document with the modules, their versions and their licences.
dependencies.why_this_one: It is CycloneDX's own Go generator, so the format is the reference implementation's rather than a re-derivation; and it emits licences as CycloneDX *evidence* (which is how the generator documents its own confidence) rather than asserting them — a distinction this repository keeps visible instead of flattening. That is why the sbom-go row does NOT pass -assert-licenses.
dependencies.alternatives: syft (multi-ecosystem, larger install, its Go support reads the built binary or the module cache rather than go.mod); `go version -m` plus a hand-written renderer (no licence data at all).
dependencies.license_check: Apache-2.0, on the allowlist. No ADR required.

not_added_deliberately.name: @cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm
not_added_deliberately.why: Evaluated for the npm face and rejected: it cannot read pnpm-lock.yaml, so against this workspace it either fails or renders an inventory of a tree the repository does not install. `pnpm sbom` reads the lockfile pnpm itself owns. There is therefore no pin for it in ops/security/tool-versions.sh — a variable nothing consumes is a pin somebody eventually installs and trusts.

not_added_deliberately.name: trivy / grype
not_added_deliberately.why: The container-scan row has no object to scan: there is no Dockerfile anywhere in this tree (ops/runbook-steps.json, tree claim `no-dockerfile`). Adding a scanner before the image would be a row that always passes. The gate's container-scan row is a guarded absence instead, and it fails the moment an image appears, which is the point at which this entry has to be filled in. See ops/security/absent-checks.json.

not_added_deliberately.name: semgrep
not_added_deliberately.why: The single-tool alternative for all three SAST faces. Rejected for V1 in favour of the per-language tools this tree already had a place for, and because its default ruleset is fetched rather than pinned — a security verdict that changes when a remote ruleset changes is not a verdict this repository can reproduce. It remains the leading candidate for post-V1 if a single tool turns out to be worth more than three pinned ones.
